economy.summary: As governor he pursued a tourism-led growth strategy whose flagship, Tinapa, later failed commercially. His main 2027 economic pledge is to price petrol for domestic use at production cost, which he puts at about ₦300 per litre.
economy.analysis:
Duke's governorship (1999-2007) predates current state economic data series, so no reliable figures were found for growth, IGR or poverty in Cross River during his tenure. His administration bet heavily on tourism and services: the Tinapa business and leisure resort, the revived Obudu Ranch and the Calabar Carnival (RECORD). He has said tourism brought about 2.3 million visitors to the state within a month. That is his own claim and is UNVERIFIED. Tinapa's later failure to trade as planned is covered under infrastructure and finance.

For 2027, his headline pledge is to cut petrol to about ₦300 per litre. Speaking on Channels Television in October 2026, he said he would price petroleum for local consumption at production and refining costs, which he estimates at about $45 a barrel, rather than at international crude prices. He would reserve part of daily crude output, for example 600,000 barrels, for domestic use (PROMISE). He has called the current arrangement a 'poorly-managed option' that replaced the earlier 'subsidy scam'. ANALYSIS: pricing crude below market for domestic refiners is an implicit subsidy. It would reduce Federation Account revenue shared with states and could revive cross-border smuggling. The sources reviewed do not show how he would finance or ring-fence it. His acceptance speech also stressed local production and import substitution, with few specifics.
strengths: Track record of pursuing a distinctive sectoral strategy (tourism)
limitations: No published costing of the crude-allocation plan
Flagship Tinapa investment did not perform commercially
unknowns: Fiscal impact of the ₦300 petrol plan

security.summary: He proposes state police and, where needed, local-government police, along with intelligence-led policing and judicial oversight. His governorship-era security record was not documented in the sources found.
security.analysis:
No sources were found evaluating security conditions in Cross River during 1999-2007. The Bakassi Peninsula transfer to Cameroon was agreed by the federal government in the 2006 Greentree Agreement while he was governor. Foreign and boundary policy was federal, and his own role and statements on it were not documented in the sources reviewed.

His 2027 proposals are more developed. In a September 2026 Arise News interview he argued that Nigeria's security architecture has barely changed since 1970. He backed state police and, where needed, local-government police, with clear guidelines and safeguards (PROMISE). He said intelligence is 'eighty per cent of security' and criticised the failure to penetrate Boko Haram after nearly two decades. He cited the US National Guard as a model of state formations within a federal framework, and he wants a stronger judiciary to oversee police conduct. He links banditry and kidnapping to poverty and the lack of legitimate jobs. When accepting the nomination, he called for stronger intelligence gathering and community-based policing. ANALYSIS: his position differs from his party's. In June 2026 the PRP rejected the federal government's state-police amendment as 'suspicious', although that objection was about who leads the reform. Any state-police model requires a constitutional amendment.
strengths: Coherent decentralised-policing position with oversight safeguards
limitations: No timeline, cost or legislative strategy found
No documented security record from his governorship
unknowns: Detailed security chapter of the PRP manifesto
His role in state responses during the Bakassi transition

education.summary: Little documented evidence exists on his education record beyond the founding of Cross River University of Technology. His 2027 education plans are unspecified in the sources reviewed.
education.analysis: Governor Bassey Otu has credited Duke with establishing the Cross River University of Technology (RECORD, as attributed by his successor's government). No enrolment, funding or outcome data from 1999-2007 were found. His 2019 platform promised compulsory education to age 18, teacher-pupil ratios of 1:20 (primary) and 1:30 (secondary), and rural hardship allowances. In 2018, Africa Check found one of his education statistics downplayed and another exaggerated. His 2026 acceptance speech listed education as a priority without detail.
limitations: No outcome data for his governorship
2027 education plans not detailed in sources reviewed
unknowns: Whether 2019 education commitments carry into the 2027 manifesto

His 2019 platform proposed raising the health budget by more than 35 per cent, universal health coverage and at least one general hospital per local government area. His 2026 acceptance speech named health as a priority without specifics. The PRP manifesto's health content was not available.

infrastructure.summary: His administration built Tinapa and revived Obudu Ranch, and made Calabar known for urban cleanliness. Tinapa was inaugurated in 2007 but later decayed and was handed to AMCON over unpaid debt. Successors and critics blame its design; Duke blames successors for abandoning it.
infrastructure.analysis:
Tinapa broke ground in 2005 on a 265-hectare site near Calabar. It was declared a federal free trade zone in August 2006 and inaugurated in April 2007 under Duke (RECORD; status commissioned). Reported costs exceed $350 million, and his successor Liyel Imoke uses the same figure. Shops were later largely empty, Customs disputed the zone's status in 2013, the state transferred 85 per cent of shares to AMCON, and EndSARS looting in 2020 damaged the hotel. Governor Otu's government took the resort back in February 2025, with no revival steps reported six months later (FACT). Imoke has said the project was 'badly conceived' and lacked the infrastructure and regulation it needed. Duke said in 2019 that successors 'did not understand the concept' and abandoned it (DISPUTED).

He also revived the pre-existing Obudu Cattle Ranch as a mountain resort. Imoke says it was funded with about ₦10 billion in state bonds and that its cable car, which he costs at about $40 million, covered only 8 per cent of its maintenance through ticket revenue (DISPUTED; Imoke's figures). In Calabar he created waste-management and urban-development agencies. A 2006 US diplomatic cable described the city as widely considered Nigeria's cleanest. Al Jazeera reported in 2022 that those standards later declined under successors.
strengths: Visible urban-management results in Calabar during his tenure
limitations: Tinapa's commercial failure and debt burden
Maintenance burden of Obudu assets after his tenure
unknowns: Audited total cost of Tinapa and Obudu works

His 2027 statements reviewed focus on petrol pricing, not electricity tariffs, grid investment, gas supply or the Electricity Act 2023 framework. jobs.summary: His jobs agenda rests on local production and support for farmers, with no targets. No employment data from his governorship were found.
jobs.analysis: Tourism was intended to create jobs in Cross River, but no employment figures for 1999-2007 were found, apart from his own unverified visitor claims. His 2019 platform aimed to cut unemployment by 15 per cent over two terms. In 2026 he called for job creation through local production and value addition, better credit access and guaranteed markets for farmers. He also linked insecurity to the lack of legitimate jobs. No numeric target or mechanism was found.
limitations: No targets or mechanisms published
unknowns: Employment effects of Tinapa and Obudu
missing: Jobs section of the PRP manifesto

finance.summary: Tinapa was financed partly by a ₦40 billion federally guaranteed bond on which the state later defaulted, and short-term bank loans funded long-term projects. How much of Cross River's later debt traces to his era is disputed.
finance.analysis:
A former DMO staff member who says he recommended the guarantee wrote in 2018 that Tinapa was backed by a ₦40 billion bond with a federal guarantee approved in 2005. He wrote that Cross River later defaulted on interest payments and the debt became an obligation to the federal government. He also said short-term commercial bank loans, secured by irrevocable standing payment orders on federal allocations, financed long-term projects including Tinapa and Obudu, and that the projects could not generate enough cash to service them (ANALYSIS by an informed but interested author). Imoke has said Tinapa debt service once took more than half of state revenues. The state later handed the asset to AMCON, which had been expected to invest ₦26-29 billion. Bayelsa Governor Douye Diri, responding in 2026 to Duke's criticism of the coastal highway, called Tinapa a 'white elephant' and urged Duke to repay its debts (DISPUTED; political claim).

On the other side, a 2015 Daily Trust report quoted a former vice-chancellor describing much of the state's debt as accumulated after Duke left office in 2007. No audited debt figure for May 2007 was found. ANALYSIS: the record shows high-risk, debt-financed public investment. How much of the burden belongs to his administration, and how much to successors' borrowing and management, is not settled.
strengths: Pre-governorship experience as state finance commissioner
limitations: Tinapa bond default and AMCON takeover
Short-term loans used for long-term assets
unknowns: Cross River debt stock at May 2007

leadership.summary: He completed two terms as governor with a strong, personally associated agenda. He has since moved between several parties, and he says he would step aside for a consensus opposition candidate.
leadership.analysis:
Duke served two full terms and handed over to his elected successor in 2007 (FACT). Accounts of his governing style describe close personal involvement. Residents told Al Jazeera that he drove around Calabar incognito to check cleanliness, and that waste workers were paid promptly while tourism was central to policy (UNVERIFIED anecdotes). Governor Otu has credited his leadership as a guide for current policy. His successor Imoke has said he 'dissected' and criticised Duke's approach (ANALYSIS: an intra-party dispute).

Since leaving office he has moved between parties several times. He left the PDP for the SDP in 2018 and won the SDP ticket after court battles that ended in his favour. He was later back in the PDP, left it again for the ADC in January 2026, and won the PRP primary in May 2026 (FACT). In November 2026 he said he would step aside for a consensus opposition candidate if parties agreed collectively. He argued that a coalition must first agree on a national vision, not just share out positions (PROMISE/statement). ANALYSIS: this conditional pledge is unusual. Voters cannot yet tell whether he will be on the final ballot as a principal contender.
strengths: Completed two terms and a peaceful handover
limitations: Frequent party changes
Coalition-building at national level untested

integrity.summary: No criminal charge or conviction was found. He was reported in 2006 as one of the few governors not on the EFCC's watch list, a challenge to his 2026 nomination was dismissed, and the criticism of his Tinapa debts is political, not legal.
integrity.analysis:
Searches found no EFCC charge, court conviction or adverse audit finding against Duke personally. A Dubawa profile notes he was described as one of the only governors not on the EFCC's 2006 watch list, a point reported by the BBC at the time according to secondary summaries (FACT as reported; primary BBC report not opened). The criticism he faces over Tinapa and state debt comes from political rivals and successors, including Imoke and Diri. It concerns policy and financing judgement, not alleged personal enrichment, and none has led to legal action that this research found (legalStatus: allegation).

In June 2026, PRP aspirant Kingsley Yakubu sued to void his nomination. Yakubu alleged that Duke's name was missing from the membership register sent to INEC, that he skipped physical screening, and that vote totals were inflated. Around 30 September 2026, the Federal High Court in Abuja dismissed the suit. Reports differ on the grounds: ThisDay says party membership was held to be an internal matter, and Premium Times says the suit was statute-barred and the claims were not proved (legalStatus: judgment). No appeal was found. Africa Check rated two of his 2018 education statistics as inaccurate. That concerns accuracy, not misconduct. No public asset declaration by Duke was found in the sources reviewed.
limitations: No public asset declaration found
Contested accuracy of some campaign statistics

experience.summary: He was a two-term governor (1999-2007), a state finance commissioner and a corporate lawyer. He has held no public office since 2007.
experience.analysis:
Duke trained as a lawyer (LL.B. from ABU in 1982, called to the Bar in 1983, LL.M. from the University of Pennsylvania in 1984) and practised corporate law in 1985-1988 (FACT). He was Cross River's commissioner for finance and budget/planning in 1992-1993. In 1997-1998 he sat on federal economic bodies, including the National Economic Intelligence Committee and the Federal Economic Council, and chaired the NAFCON privatisation committee, according to his firm's biography (FACT, self-published). He was governor from 1999 to 2007, winning 529,335 votes in 1999 according to reference summaries, and won re-election in 2003. He received the CON national honour in 2008.

ANALYSIS: his executive experience is real but nearly two decades old. It predates the current fiscal federalism, the post-2023 subsidy and exchange-rate reforms, and the scale of present insecurity. He has no federal executive or legislative service. His 2019 presidential run won 34,746 votes, so he has not yet built a national electoral base. His record as governor offers both a model of focused urban management and a cautionary case in debt-financed megaprojects, and both are relevant to national office.
strengths: Two terms of state executive experience
limitations: No public office since 2007
No federal executive experience

strengths: Clear headline positions on fuel and policing

foreign.analysis: Duke holds an LL.M. from the University of Pennsylvania and promoted Tinapa and the Calabar Carnival partly to attract international visitors and investors. No positions on ECOWAS, the Sahel, trade or diaspora policy were found.

humanImpact.summary: Residents remember a clean, well-run Calabar during his tenure. The debts from his flagship projects constrained later state budgets, and Tinapa's decline removed expected jobs and services.
humanImpact.analysis:
For Calabar residents, the most cited effect of his tenure is urban cleanliness and order. Traders and civic campaigners told Al Jazeera in 2022 that refuse was rarely seen on the roads, bins were placed about every 100 metres and collectors were paid promptly. They compared this with later conditions, when refuse piled up at Watts Market and collectors boycotted over unpaid wages (UNVERIFIED recollections; the later decline occurred under successors). A 2006 US diplomatic cable recorded the city's reputation as Nigeria's cleanest.

The longer-term household cost is harder to measure. If Tinapa and Obudu debts were serviced from federal allocations, as a former DMO official and Imoke have described, they would have reduced money available for salaries and services after 2007. Imoke estimated Tinapa's cost at close to $170 per Cross River resident (ANALYSIS/DISPUTED). Tinapa's empty shops and looted hotel also meant the expected employment did not materialise at scale. For 2027, his ₦300 petrol pledge is aimed directly at household transport and food costs. He cites the ₦70,000 minimum wage being consumed by fuel. Its distributional effects depend on financing details not yet published.
strengths: Documented improvement in urban environment during tenure
limitations: Debt burden passed to later administrations
No household-level data from 1999-2007
unknowns: Cross River poverty and service-access data for his tenure

promises.summary: His 2027 promises (₦300 petrol, state police, opposition unity) are clear in direction but mostly lack targets, timelines and costs. No independent tracking of his 1999-2007 promises was found.
promises.analysis:
For his governorship there is no independent tracker comparing 1999 and 2003 campaign promises with delivery. His flagship projects (Tinapa, Obudu, the Calabar Carnival) were delivered to the point of operation within his tenure. Their long-run sustainability is disputed (RECORD).

As a 2027 aspirant, his most specific promise is the ₦300 petrol price, with a stated mechanism: domestic crude priced at production cost and a share of output, such as 600,000 barrels a day, reserved for local consumption (PROMISE). It has no published timeline or fiscal estimate. His state and local-government police proposal names safeguards (judicial oversight, guidelines) but has no timeline. His June 2026 agenda names priorities without targets. He has made a conditional commitment to step aside for a consensus opposition candidate if parties agree collectively (PROMISE). That commitment is unusual and can be checked against events. His 2019 platform contained more quantified pledges, including a 15 per cent unemployment cut over two terms, specific teacher ratios and a health budget increase of more than 35 per cent. It is unclear whether these carry into the 2027 manifesto. ANALYSIS: on the evidence available, his 2027 promises are less specific than his 2019 ones.
limitations: No timelines or costs for main pledges
